'''Ankoku-ji''' (安国寺) or '''Ankoku Zenji''' is a temple of the [[Myōshin-ji sect]] located in [[Chino, Nagano]], Nagano Prefecture, Japan. It is situated in the Ankokuji area of Miyagawa and is dedicated to [[Shakyamuni Tathāgata]]. The temple's mountain name (''sangō'') is Taihei-zan. Ankoku-ji was founded during the [[Nanboku-chō period]] as one of the [[Ankoku-ji]], a network of temples established by the [[Ashikaga clan]].
== History ==
The temple was founded in [[Ryakuō]] 4 (1341) as part of the [[Ankoku-ji]], a network of temples built during the [[Nanboku-chō period]] by [[Ashikaga Takauji]] and his brother [[Ashikaga Tadayoshi]]. Its establishment in [[Shinano Province]] was facilitated by [[Suwa Enchū]], an official of the [[Ashikaga shogunate]].
The original temple featured a full set of seven halls (''shichidō garan'') and included eight sub-temples (''tatchū''), such as Eikan-ji, Todō-ji, Nōkun-ji, Onkō-ji, Shōgan-ji, Sanshō-ji, Kongō-ji, and Taishō-ji. It was located near the Mae-miya, the shrine associated with the [[Suwa-taisha]] Upper Shrine. The area around the temple developed as a temple town, with neighborhoods such as Higashi-Ōmachi and Nishi-Ōmachi forming nearby.
In [[Bunmei]] 12 (1480), the temple was damaged by fire during conflicts between the Upper and Lower Shrines of Suwa. Two years later, a major flood of the [[Miya River]] washed away much of the temple complex, leaving it in ruins. In [[Tenbun]] 11 (1542), the temple suffered further destruction during the [[Battle of Miyagawa]]. During the [[:en:Anei|Anei]] era, the temple was relocated and rebuilt at its current site, with support from the [[Suwa Domain]], and was affiliated with the [[Myōshin-ji]].
The temple's crest (''kamon'') combines the Ashikaga clan's double-bar crest and the [[Suwa clan's kaji-no-ha crest]].
=== City-Designated Historic Site ===
The temple grounds include the "Suwa Clan Ankoku-ji Mausoleum," designated as a city historic site. The mausoleum contains gravestones and [[Hōkyōintō]] inscribed with the posthumous names of [[Suwa Mitsuchika]] and his wife, as well as a memorial for his brother, [[Suwa Yoritaka]]. The mausoleum received regular upkeep and funding from the Suwa Domain during the [[Edo period]]. Although a typhoon in 1959 damaged the structure, many elements remain intact.<ref>Historical marker for the Suwa Clan Ankoku-ji Mausoleum, Chino City.</ref>
Close to the mausoleum is the "Hisawa Castle Ruins," also a city-designated historic site. Hisawa Castle, also called Ankoku-ji Castle, played a significant role in defending the nearby Mae-miya Shrine.<ref>Historical marker for the Hisawa Castle Ruins, Chino City.</ref>
